title: The information trail of the 'Freshman 15' - A systematic review of a health myth within the research and popular literature
screen_reason: Although titled a 'systematic review', the study is a content analysis of a keyword-defined corpus of popular-press articles (19 magazine, 146 general newspaper, 141 university newspaper, 1985-2006) judged against an external ground truth (14 peer-reviewed studies, 1,858 students, mean gain 4.6 lb) for whether they accurately depict freshman weight gain. It reports a quantitative share with a denominator: '42% of the articles published in magazine and newspapers' reflected the research accurately, the remainder promulgating the 15-pound myth. This is a CONTENT estimate, but it is reported in the ACCURATE direction only — see the borderline flag and notes.

estimates.platform: Magazines, general-readership newspapers and university newspapers (indexed in 23 bibliographic databases)
estimates.date: Articles published 1985-2006 (university newswire articles restricted to January 1997-December 2006); database searches run in/around late November 2007
estimates.measure_type: % of popular-press (magazine and newspaper) articles about the 'Freshman 15' that ACCURATELY reflected the research finding of less-than-15-pound freshman weight gain (inverse of the misinformation share; complement not computed per R8)
estimates.value_raw: 42% of the articles published in magazine and newspapers reflected the research finding with accuracy; 'the other approximately 150 popular press articles warn readers of the fateful 15 pounds'
estimates.denominator: Magazine and newspaper articles about the 'Freshman 15'/freshman weight gain retrieved from 23 databases, 1985-2006 (19 magazine + 146 general newspaper + 141 university newspaper = 306 popular-press articles of the 333 total); the denominator is not printed alongside the 42%
estimates.definition: An article was accurate if it reflected the research finding that American and Canadian first-year students gain less than the purported 15 pounds; the remainder 'warn readers of the fateful 15 pounds', i.e. assert a 15-pound gain the evidence does not support
estimates.misinfo_def: the widely held health belief, but not substantiated scientific fact: the ‘Freshman 15’ … unsubstantiated and/or embellished health information
estimates.n: 306 popular-press articles (19 magazine, 146 general newspaper, 141 university newspaper); exact denominator for the 42% not stated
estimates.source_quote: Examination of the scholarly research on freshman weight gain indicated that, although American and Canadian first-year college and university students do gain weight, it is less than the purported ‘Freshman 15’. This finding is reflected with accuracy by 42% of the articles published in magazine and newspapers. Although the other approximately 150 popular press articles warn readers of the fateful 15 pounds, it was surprising to observe that the information presented was not entirely alarmist in nature.
estimates.page_loc: Conclusions, p. 9 (Health Information and Libraries Journal 25:1-12)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single author (C. Brown) read each retrieved article and coded its stance on freshman weight gain (fact or myth) plus information types, judging accuracy against the 14 peer-reviewed studies she had assembled (1,858 subjects, mean gain 4.6 lb). No codebook, no second coder and no inter-rater reliability statistic are reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: To assess the accuracy and validity of the information presented in the articles appearing in the popular press, contents of the relevant magazine and newspaper articles were reviewed for the types of information published including expert and/or anecdotal information, the article’s stance on freshman weight gain (fact or myth), as well as information about nutrition, exercise, health and alcohol consumption.
estimates.notes: POLARITY WARNING for the adjudicator: the value is the ACCURATE share, not the misinformation share. The misinformation share (~58%) is a complement I would have to compute and is therefore not extracted per R8. The paper's own figures are internally inconsistent: 42% of 306 popular-press articles = ~129 accurate, which would leave ~177 inaccurate, not the 'approximately 150' stated; the abstract instead says 'half of the popular press publications claimed a 15-pound (6.804 kg) weight gain', and 'about half of the newspaper articles did not debunk the ‘Freshman 15’ theory'. Note also that 42% is the same figure the paper uses two paragraphs later for a different quantity ('writers of American and Canadian university newspapers were responsible for 42% of the articles', i.e. 141/333 = 42.3%), which raises the possibility that the accuracy 42% is a transcription error. year set to 2006, the last publication year in the corpus (corpus spans 1985-2006); searches run around late November 2007, publication 2008. breadth coded 'false' because the classification turns on a specific false quantitative claim (15 lb vs a measured 4.6 lb mean), even though the extracted numerator is the accurate side. QUOTE NOTE: the sentence is quoted exactly as printed in the paper (Conclusions), but the PDF text layer collapses inter-word spaces on two of its lines ('thepurported‘Freshman15’.Thisfindingisreflected'), so the quote is not a contiguous byte span in the text file. The value-bearing clause 'with accuracy by 42% of the articles published in magazine and newspapers' does match verbatim; quote_verbatim=false records the defect.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'only six of the magazine articles definitively called the ‘Freshman 15’ a myth' against a verbatim denominator of 19 magazine articles gives an exact 6/19 = 31.6% debunking share, but its complement is explicitly NOT all misinformation ('The other articles either forthrightly stated that the phenomena was real, was underestimated or gave no opinion on the issue'), so no row was created. (2) The abstract's 'half of the popular press publications claimed a 15-pound (6.804 kg) weight gain' and the results' 'about half of the newspaper articles did not debunk the ‘Freshman 15’ theory' are verbal quantifiers with no count or stated denominator — not extractable as point values. (3) Table 3 carries per-article Fact/Myth checkmarks for the 19 magazine articles and Figures 3 and 4 are yes/no content-analysis bar charts for the 146 general and 141 university newspaper articles; counting the marks myself would be my coding, not the paper's stated value, so these were not converted into rows. (4) 'A small number of articles (2%) in other types of publications' refers to publication type, not veracity. (5) The 14 peer-reviewed studies' weight-gain means (Table 2) are effect sizes about weight, not misinformation shares.

rob.design: Single-author content analysis framed as a systematic review: keyword-index search of 23 bibliographic databases (via First Search, OVID and PubMed) for 'freshman 15' OR 'freshman weight gain', articles 1985-2006 (LexisNexis university newswire 1997-2006 only); records de-duplicated in Excel, full text obtained and screened for relevance by the author; 333 articles retained (20 peer-reviewed, 19 magazine, 146 newspaper, 141 university newspaper, ~2% other); popular-press articles coded by the author alone for stance (fact/myth) and information type; no codebook, second coder, inter-rater reliability or denominators for the headline percentage are reported; English-language only.
